procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (convicted the appellants under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and imposed a fine of Rs. 1000/- each, and sentenced them to 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 06.08.2021 of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal Appeal No. 228 of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a Criminal Appeal (No. 228 of 2015) before the High Court of Judicature at Madras challenging their conviction by the Trial Court. The High Court confirmed the conviction and the fine but reduced the sentence of 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment to 5 years Rigorous Imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court, after considering the facts and circumstances, was convinced that the High Court's judgment required interference. The Supreme Court noted that there were no allegations of repeated or severe blows and that the injuries were simple in nature. The appeal was disposed of.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction of the appellants stands modified to that under Sections 323 and 324 of the IPC.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence imposed is reduced to the period already undergone. The fine imposed is maintained.
directions: The appellants stand discharged of the liabilities of their bail bonds, if any.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Courts below were justified in convicting the appellants under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, when the victims had sustained simple injuries.

facts: The victims, PW1 and his mother PW2, sustained only simple injuries, as confirmed by the doctor (PW13).
The injuries were not on any vital part of the body.
The appellants (accused Nos. 3 and 4) were armed with knives and attempted to attack PW1, but he escaped the main attack.
PW1's injuries were abrasions sustained when he caught hold of the appellants' hands.
There was no allegation of repeated or severe blows being inflicted on the victims.
A pre-existing civil dispute over a lane existed between the complainant (PW1) and accused No. 1.
law: To sustain a conviction under Section 307 IPC (attempt to murder), it is not necessary that a bodily injury capable of causing death should have been inflicted.
The essential element is the 'intention or knowledge' to cause death, irrespective of the result of the act.
The court must ascertain the accused's intention from the surrounding circumstances.
Factors to consider when inferring intent include the nature of the weapon used, the severity of the blows, and the nature of the actual injury, if any.
application: The Court acknowledged the legal principle that simple injuries alone do not automatically negate a charge under Section 307 IPC.
However, it examined the surrounding circumstances to determine the appellants' actual intent.

The Court found that several factors indicated a lack of intention to kill: the injuries were simple, there were no repeated or severe blows, and the appellants, though armed with knives, did not ensure the death of the complainant when they had the opportunity.
The fact that the injuries were simple was considered an 'additional point in the appellants’ favour' when assessing their intent.
Based on these circumstances, the Court concluded that the evidence on record did not establish the requisite intention or knowledge to cause death.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction under Section 307 IPC was unsustainable. It held that the facts of the case only made out offenses under Sections 323 (voluntarily causing hurt) and 324 (voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons) of the IPC, and accordingly modified the conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Courts below were justified in convicting the appellants under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, when the victims had sustained simple injuries.
appellant_arguments: The conviction under Section 307 of the IPC is unsustainable based on the materials on record, and only offenses under Sections 323 and 324 of the IPC can be made out.
respondent_arguments: The appellants being armed with knives clearly indicates their intention to kill, and it was only due to providence that the victims' lives were saved, thus justifying the conviction under Section 307.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for attempt to murder under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is unsustainable when the materials on record only make out the lesser offenses of voluntarily causing hurt under Sections 323 and 324 of the IPC.
obiter: A shoots at Z with intention to kill him, under such circumstances that, if death ensued, A would be guilty of murder. A is liable to punishment under this section.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that a conviction under Section 307 of the IPC was unsustainable because the evidence did not support an intention to kill, as there was no allegation of repeated or severe blows having been inflicted, and the injuries sustained by the victims were simple in nature. These facts warranted a modification of the conviction to lesser offenses under Sections 323 and 324 of the IPC.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a conviction under Section 307 IPC is justified, the court analyzes the nature of the attack and the resulting injuries to infer the accused's intent. The absence of repeated or severe blows and the finding that injuries are simple in nature are factors that weigh against establishing an intention to cause death.
